newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Cheung Kong wins praise after restructuring.
newsitem.headline: Cheung Kong wins praise after restructuring.

text.p: The reorganisation of Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd won good marks from analysts on Tuesday for streamlining the group even though the massive deal involved few new assets or strategic ideas.
"It gives a much clearer picture to the overall grouping and restructures the group to make better use of resources and assets," said Mark Simpson, head of Hong Kong research at ING Barings.
Hong Kong billionaire Li Ka-shing's flagship business group announced the major corporate restructuring on Monday affecting his China infrastructure firm and Hong Kong electricity utility.

The restructuring consists of two major moves and involves all four of the group's listed companies, parent Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd, its 45 percent-held associate Hutchison Whampoa, Hong Kong Electric Holdings Ltd and the newest member of the group, Cheung Kong Infrastructure Holdings Ltd
Hutchison led off by acquiring additional shares in Hongkong Electric, pushing its stake in the utility over the 35 percent mark and triggering a general offer at HK$26.25 per share.

Hutchison will transfer its 35.01 percent holding and any other shares it receives in the general offer, up to a 50.01 percent stake, to Cheung Kong Infrastructure (CKI). Cheung Kong will transfer its 70.66 percent stake in CKI to Hutchison.
Previously, Cheung Kong controlled CKI, while Cheung Kong's 45-percent-owned associate Hutchison controlled Hongkong Electric.
Now the line of control will run more smoothly from Cheung Kong to 50.2-percent-held Hutchison to CKI to Hongkong Electric.

The structure of assets and management expertise is also smoother with the property developer and holding company controlling the conglomerate, which controls the infrastructure firm, which controls the utility, analysts said.
The timing of the reorganisation was also seen as exemplary.

The group is seeking a greater stake in Hongkong Electric at a relatively low price of HK$26.25, while parent Cheung Kong is selling its stake in China-oriented CKI at the high price earnings ratio of 27 times 1996 earnings.
"The parent company was the biggest winner," said Steven Brown, group head of research at NAVA SC Securities.
"The valuation of these infrastructure stocks is ludicrous," Brown said, adding he thought Cheung Kong felt CKI shares were overpriced in the market.
CKI shares were offered at HK$12.65 and listed in June. They closed on Friday at HK$21.15, a gain of 67.2 percent in little more than six months.

"It is difficult to say at what price Cheung Kong carried the CKI assets (before the listing), but I am forecasting that it will book an exceptional gain of HK$4.1 billion," said Manfred Ho, senior investment analyst at CEF GC Securities.
Conditions of the reorganisation, including shareholder and exchange approval, are expected to be fulfilled by May 31.
The exceptional gain will be booked in 1997 earnings, Ho said, bringing total earnings to HK$17 billion for Cheung Kong.
"This is the first time in the 20 years that Li Ka-shing has owned Hutchison that he will be able to consolidate Hutchison's earnings," said Brown.
"The question is why is he doing it?," said Brown. "Why does he want to bloat Cheung Kong's balance sheet?"
Analysts said there likely would be a second and third part to the reorganisation. But for now they appear content with the impact of the new structure on parent Cheung Kong.
"Cheung Kong was our top pick among the developers before the announcement and this deal further cements that recommendation," said Andrew Taylor, property analyst at Asia Equity.
